findings.problem: The section carries no ma_vs_federal entries at all, so a Massachusetts candidate is not told that the federal ordering-record duties it teaches are also Massachusetts duties, nor that Massachusetts adds a record of its own touching Form 222 practice.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires registered persons to keep records in conformance with the federal record-keeping requirements, and 247 CMR 9.19(9)(b) requires a pharmacy to post or keep readily retrievable the current power of attorney forms required for DEA 222 forms. Neither point falls inside the section's declared learning objectives, which are wholly federal and say nothing about signature authority, so this is a completeness observation rather than a criterion failure: nothing the section says about Massachusetts law is wrong, because it says nothing.

findings.problem: The section states that a supplier may not endorse an electronic order to another supplier to fill, but never states the paper counterpart, under which a DEA Form 222 made out to a supplier who cannot fill it within the time limit in 21 CFR 1305.13 may be endorsed to a second supplier for filling.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1305.23 prohibits endorsement of an electronic order while 21 CFR 1305.14(a) expressly permits endorsement of a paper form, and that difference is one of the route-specific duties the section's own objective 5 undertakes to identify. The statement as written is literally correct and is tagged to the CSOS rule, so a careful reader is not misled; the omission is a gap in the paper and electronic contrast rather than a misstatement, and endorsement is not named in any declared objective.

results.summary: Every proposition in the section was checked against the current text of 21 CFR part 1305 subparts A, B and C, 21 CFR 1300.01(b) and 21 CFR 1304.33(c). The section is accurate throughout. The seven exceptions in 1305.03 are complete and correctly stated. The 60-day window is correctly anchored to the purchaser's execution, correctly identified as calendar days, and correctly paired with its only exception in 1305.13(f). The defect rule in 1305.15 and the lost-form rule in 1305.16 are kept apart with the right cures, the right statements and the right carve-out for losses in the course of transmission. The retention rules are correctly split between 1305.17 for paper and subpart C for electronic orders, and the deeming rule in 1305.17(e) is correctly resolved through the defined term in 1300.01(b) rather than treated as a storage-segregation rule. The supplier-side duties, including the close-of-month copy to DEA owed by a supplier outside ARCOS and the pharmacy's ability to occupy the supplier's side under 1305.06(b) and (c), are correctly attributed, and 1304.33(c) confirms that a pharmacy registered only to dispense is not an ARCOS reporter. All six mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it. Two Low observations are recorded: the section has no Massachusetts content at all, and the paper counterpart to the electronic no-endorsement rule is not stated. Neither falls inside the section's declared objectives and neither would mislead a candidate on Massachusetts facts, so the section is publishable exactly as it stands.

findings.problem: The section presents the inventory entry for damaged, defective or impure stock, quality-control stock and extemporaneous-compounding stock as three elements, namely the name, the total quantity and the reason the substance is being maintained, but 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iv)(C) requires the reason together with whether the substance is capable of use in the manufacture of any controlled substance in finished form.
findings.rationale: The omitted clause is part of the same subparagraph the section incorporates for dispensers through 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6), and the section presents its list as the content the paragraph calls for. For a retail pharmacy the omitted answer is almost always negative, so the gap would not change any inventory or recordkeeping decision on Massachusetts facts; it is an incompleteness in an enumerated content list rather than a misstatement of the rule.

results.summary: The federal half was checked against the current text of 21 CFR 1304.04 and 1304.11, 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) and 21 CFR 1301.12(a), and the Massachusetts half against M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 7(a) and 15, 247 CMR 9.21(8) and 247 CMR 11.05 and 11.06 in the official mass.gov texts. Everything checks out. The general inventory requirements, the opening-or-close-of-business notation, the initial inventory anchored to the date activity begins with its zero-stock sentence, and the biennial interval measured from the previous biennial inventory date are all stated as the regulation states them. The opened-container counting rule is correctly confined to a commercial container that has been opened, with the more-than-1,000 tablets-or-capsules threshold correctly kept inside the Schedule III to V branch and Schedules I and II correctly left outside the estimation rule at any container size. The treatment of 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) is careful and right: the statutory general-physical-inventory clause directs the rulemaker and is not a six-month extension of the regulatory two years. The clause-by-clause reading of 1304.04(a), including the central-records notification in triplicate by registered or certified mail and the 14 days after receipt by the Special Agent in Charge, is exact, as is the point that the opening exception is about location rather than duration. On the Massachusetts side 247 CMR 11.06 was verified word for word: a pharmacy and an outsourcing facility run two years from January 1 of each even-numbered year and a wholesale druggist one year from December 1, which matches the statutory pattern in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a). All seven mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted. One Low observation is recorded about an incomplete content list for stock that is not in finished form for dispensing; it would not mislead a candidate on Massachusetts facts.

findings.problem: The section establishes that a Board-licensed retail pharmacy is not a registrant of the Department, and so is outside 105 CMR 700.005(B), from 105 CMR 700.001 and 700.004(A)(1) read with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a). That is right for the pharmacy as an entity, but the section does not mention 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(f), under which an individual pharmacist is among the practitioners required to be registered under 700.004(A)(1) and so can be a registrant of the Department in his or her own right.
findings.rationale: The entity-level conclusion is textually correct: the only appearance of the phrase retail drug business anywhere in 105 CMR 700.000 is the exclusion in 700.004(A)(1), and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every pharmacy to the Board. The section is also carefully hedged, saying the Department provisions do not reach a Board-licensed pharmacy in that capacity and pointing a Board-licensed pharmacy at the Department's requirements through the where-applicable clause of 247 CMR 20.03(7), so it does not assert that nobody at a retail pharmacy can owe a Department duty. Naming 700.004(A)(2)(f) would close the one gap a careful candidate could notice; its absence does not make anything the section says wrong.

results.summary: This is the longest section in the batch and it holds up paragraph by paragraph. 247 CMR 9.21 was read in full from the official mass.gov text and every one of its twelve paragraphs is reported accurately, including the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, the 14-day and two-year video retention, the floor-to-ceiling barrier for a pharmacy inside another retail establishment, direct delivery of drug orders, the allocation of security responsibility and access control to the Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty, the ten-day Schedule II reconciliation with the Manager of Record investigation, the restriction on who may enter or adjust the perpetual inventory, the disposal record in 9.21(9), the application of the whole section to expired, quarantined and pending-reverse-distribution stock, the non-resident carve-out in 9.21(11) and the institutional sterile compounding referral in 9.21(12). The federal half is equally exact. 21 CFR 1301.76(b) supplies both clocks and all six significance factors; the section correctly identifies the two sentences of 21 CFR 1301.74(c) that have no counterpart in 1301.76(b) and correctly reverses the in-transit allocation for a retail pharmacy under 1301.76(d); 21 U.S.C. 802(21) was checked and does name a pharmacy and a hospital as practitioners. The disposal material is right down to the paragraph level: the closed list in 1317.05(a)(1) to (4) with the standing authorisation in (a)(5), self-transport to a destruction location confined to non-practitioners by 1317.05(b)(4), the 30 calendar days and the no-re-routing and personal-receipt controls in 1317.15, the comingling and unknown-substance sentences in 1317.90(b), the defined term in 1300.05, the four destinations in 1317.95 with their two-employee procedures, and the DEA Form 41 attached by 1304.21(e) only to destruction under 1317.95(d) and to causing destruction under 1317.95(c), with the immediate-administration exception. The order-form point is also correct: 1305.03(f) excepts distributions to reverse distributors by collectors and law enforcement, not a pharmacy emptying its own shelf, so the Schedule II movement runs on an order form the pharmacy fills, retains under 1305.17(b) and copies to DEA at the close of the month under 1305.13(d). The three Massachusetts theft-or-loss routes were each verified in the official text: 247 CMR 20.03(7), M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 second paragraph, and 105 CMR 700.008, along with the waiver in 105 CMR 700.140 and the screening and employment provisions in 105 CMR 700.005(B). All six mapped practice questions are answerable and none is contradicted. One Low observation is recorded about a nuance of Department registrant scope that the section does not name; it does not affect any conclusion the section reaches.

findings.problem: The section teaches that the five-year records duty in 247 CMR 20.02(4) does not bind a non-resident pharmacy, on the ground that 247 CMR 20.02(5) switches off the whole of 247 CMR 20.02 for it. 247 CMR 20.02(5) carves out only the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02, and 20.02(4) is a records-retention requirement rather than a reporting requirement, so on the better reading it survives for a non-resident pharmacy through 247 CMR 20.07(1).
findings.rationale: Three textual points run against the section. First, 247 CMR 20.02(5) reads that the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies, and those restrictive words identify a subset of what 20.02 contains rather than the whole of it. Second, the Board shows elsewhere in the same body of regulations that it knows how to switch a whole section off: 247 CMR 9.21(11) reads that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.21 do not apply to non-resident pharmacies, with no narrowing word at all. Third, 247 CMR 20.07(1) affirmatively requires a non-resident pharmacy to comply with all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 unless otherwise provided, so a provision that is not carved out stays on it. The section also glosses 20.07(1) as keeping all other provisions, or the rest, of 247 CMR 20.00 on a non-resident pharmacy, which builds the contested reading into the paraphrase, and it states the narrower and correct reading in one place of its own, at comparison_tables[2].rows[1].cells[2], which describes 20.02(5) as switching off the reporting requirements in the whole of 247 CMR 20.02. The practical consequence points toward under-retention: worked_examples[4] is built on a Manager of Record who plans to purge the pharmacy's file two years after the Board report goes in, and the section corrects only the reporting trigger while telling the candidate that the five-year provision belongs to a rule that does not apply. A candidate applying that to Massachusetts facts could destroy records relating to a reported improper dispensing three years early. The defect is confined to the scope of one carve-out; the reporting duty, the recipient and the discovery-of-the-improper-dispensing trigger under 247 CMR 20.07(3) are all stated correctly, so a short correction cures it.

findings.problem: Learning objective 10 undertakes to route a theft, loss or suspected tampering to every recipient Massachusetts names, but the section never states the duty in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 under which a person registered to dispense who must file a DEA Form 106 files a copy simultaneously with the police department in the city or town where the theft or loss is alleged to have occurred and with the department of state police. The police appear only inside the quoted text of 247 CMR 20.03(7).
findings.rationale: The declared subtopic limits the section to the Massachusetts theft or loss reports to the Board and to the Drug Control Program, and the section expressly assigns the federal theft-or-loss route to another section, so the police leg is arguably outside its declared scope; the quotation of 247 CMR 20.03(7) also names the state and local police among the requirements to comply with where applicable. The objective nevertheless promises more than the body delivers, which is why this is recorded rather than passed over in silence.

findings.problem: MA-Q-0369 puts the 24-hour duty in 105 CMR 700.008 on a Massachusetts pharmacy, while the section teaches that a retail drug business is registered with the Board rather than the Department and that the 24-hour route reaches an operator such as a hospital directly.
findings.rationale: The question remains answerable from the section and is not contradicted by it. The section supplies the recipient, the instrument, the 24-hour period and the discovery trigger, and its own worked_examples[2] runs the identical facts to the identical answer using the word registrant for the actor. Every distractor in the question is eliminated by the section's own teaching, including the wrong recipient, the wrong start date, the no-report-without-confirmation answer and the wait-for-the-investigation answer. The section also states that 247 CMR 20.03(7) points a Board-licensed pharmacy at the Department's requirements where applicable, so it does not tell a candidate that a pharmacy owes nothing. The friction is one of wording between the stem's actor and the section's careful use of the defined term, and it does not defeat the mapping.

results.summary: 247 CMR 15.00 and 247 CMR 20.00 were read in full from the official mass.gov texts, and almost everything in this section is exact. The six minimum CQI provisions in 15.02(1)(a) to (f), the split in 15.03(1) between the escalation duty on all pharmacy personnel and the pharmacist's three-part immediate response with the professional-judgment qualifier attached to the prescriber alone, the 24-hour documentation deadline with its four content elements, the analysis and response halves of 15.03(3), and the four paragraphs of 15.04 including the two years measured from the date of the QRE report are all reported as the regulation states them. On the reporting side, the two seven-business-day duties in 20.02(1) and (2) are correctly separated by event, recipients and trigger; the three recipients of a serious adverse drug event report are right; 20.02(3) and the five-year readily retrievable retention in 20.02(4) are right; 247 CMR 20.03(7) and 247 CMR 20.07(1) and (3) are quoted accurately and the contrast between the resident and the non-resident trigger, which is the heart of the section, is correct. 105 CMR 700.008 and 105 CMR 700.140 were verified word for word, as were the definition of Registrant in 105 CMR 700.001 and the exclusion in 105 CMR 700.004(A)(1). One Medium defect prevents a KEEP. The section teaches that the five-year retention in 247 CMR 20.02(4) does not bind a non-resident pharmacy because 20.02(5) switches off the whole of 20.02, but 20.02(5) carves out only the reporting requirements in 247 CMR 20.02, 247 CMR 20.07(1) keeps all provisions of 247 CMR 20.00 on a non-resident pharmacy unless otherwise provided, and the Board's unqualified wording in 247 CMR 9.21(11) shows how it switches a whole section off when it means to. The teaching appears in a comparison-table cell and on the resolution path of a worked example built on a proposal to purge a file at two years, so it points a candidate toward destroying records three years early. Two Low observations are also recorded. Nine mapped practice questions were checked; all are answerable from the section and none is contradicted, so practice_mapping_verdict is PASS.
